transcript.content: Hi, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. Well, I came in because my head just doesn’t stay on task anymore. It's getting pretty frustrating. Like, I’ll be at work doing inventory, or trying to study for my supervisor certification, and I just keep reading the same line over and over. Or I'll walk into the supply closet and completely forget what I even went in there for. I just can't seem to focus on anything.
Have you noticed these problems with focus and forgetfulness since you were a child, or is this something that started more recently as an adult?

No, definitely not since I was a kid. It's... it's a lot more recent than that. I'd say this has been going on for about three years now. 

It started right around the time the contractor I work for changed our schedules. They put us on these rotating evening and overnight shifts at some of the larger properties we clean, and that's really when I started noticing it.
On your days off, when you're not working the rotating evening or overnight shifts, do you find that your sleep and ability to concentrate improve?

Not really, no. My sleep has just been messed up for a long time now, whether I'm off or not. Like, after an overnight shift, I’ll get home and just lie in bed... I'm completely tired, but I'm just wired, you know? And honestly, even on my days off when I do manage to sleep a decent number of hours, I still wake up feeling like I barely rested at all. So my focus doesn't really get any better.
Has anyone told you that you snore loudly or that you seem to stop breathing or gasp for air while you're sleeping?

No, I've never had anyone tell me that. I mean, I live alone, so there's no one really around to notice if I snore or do anything weird like that while I'm sleeping. But as far as I know, no, nothing like that.
Have you noticed any other changes like unexplained weight gain, feeling unusually cold, dry skin, or hair thinning over the past few years?

No, I haven't noticed any of that. My weight has been pretty much the same, and I haven't had any issues with feeling cold or changes with my skin or hair. None of those things really ring a bell for me.
On the nights when you try to sleep at a normal nighttime hour, completely unrelated to any upcoming shift, do you still have trouble falling or staying asleep?

Yeah, like I was saying earlier, it doesn't really matter what kind of schedule I'm on. My sleep has just been messed up for a long time now. 

The tired but wired thing is definitely worse right after an overnight shift, but even on a normal night when I try to sleep regular hours... I mean, even if I do manage to sleep a decent number of hours, I still wake up feeling like I barely rested. So yeah, I just always have trouble getting actual rest, no matter what time I go to bed.
If you take a week or more off from work altogether, with no shifts at all, does your sleep and daytime alertness return to normal during that time?

No, not really. I took a week off around the holidays last year, and I thought maybe I'd finally catch up on my sleep. But honestly, it didn't change much. I still tossed and turned, and I still felt just as drained during the day. It's like my body just forgot how to actually rest, even when I don't have to worry about work.
Do you ever notice uncomfortable, crawling, or tingling sensations in your legs at night, or has anyone mentioned that you kick or jerk your legs while you sleep?

No, I don't get any weird feelings like that in my legs. No tingling or crawling or anything. And, well, nobody has ever mentioned that I kick or jerk around in my sleep, either. So I don't think that's happening.

When you have complete freedom to choose your sleep schedule, like during that week off, if you let yourself fall asleep whenever your body naturally wanted to—even if that meant sleeping during the day instead of at night—do you find you actually sleep well and feel rested during that stretch?

No, not really. Even when I had that week off and could just sleep whenever I wanted, it didn't seem to make a difference. I'd try sleeping during the day or at night, whatever felt right, but I still never woke up feeling rested. It's just the same tired feeling, no matter what time I actually manage to fall asleep.
How much caffeine, energy drinks, or other stimulants do you typically consume in a day, and does that amount change depending on whether you're working a shift or not?

I don't really drink much caffeine, to be honest. Maybe just a cup of coffee in the morning to try and get going, but that's about it. I don't touch energy drinks or anything like that. And it's pretty much the same whether I'm working or not. It doesn't seem to help much anyway, so I just stick to the one cup.
Over the past few months, have you noticed a persistent low mood, loss of interest in things you used to enjoy, or feelings of hopelessness?

Yeah, I have. Most days, it just feels like there's this heavy, flat feeling following me around. It doesn't really go away. Even when I'm just at work, you know, pushing my cleaning cart down an empty hallway, it's right there with me. Or... even if I'm sitting at home with my family, just trying to act normal. It's just this constant, low feeling all the time.

You mentioned this low, flat feeling has been following you around—how long would you say you've been feeling this way, has it been more like a few weeks to months, or has it been going on almost continuously for two years or more?

It's definitely been more than two years. I'd say... it's been going on for about three years now. Yeah, about three years. It started right around the time the contractor changed us to rotating evening and overnight shifts at the larger properties. It's just been pretty continuous since then.
Besides the low, flat mood, have you noticed a loss of interest or pleasure in activities you used to enjoy, or any feelings of worthlessness or guilt?

Well, I don't know if I'd call it guilt, but... I definitely feel like I'm not measuring up. I keep telling myself that other guys would have adjusted to this schedule by now and probably moved up to something better. But I'm still just trying not to miss the small things at work, you know, just trying to keep my head above water. It really makes me feel like maybe I'm just not cut out for anything more than this.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in activities you used to enjoy, like hobbies or spending time with family, over these past few months?

Yeah, I definitely have. I used to always make time for family get-togethers, or even these neighborhood clean-ups, but... I've just been skipping them lately. I don't really have the drive for it anymore. And it's kind of bleeding into everything else, too. Like at work, I still get the cleaning done, but I'm a lot slower now. I end up second-guessing my logs so much that I've actually just stopped pushing for the supervisor track altogether. I just don't have it in me right now.

Over these past three years, has there ever been a stretch of two weeks or more where your mood, energy, or sleep got noticeably worse than your usual baseline—maybe with big changes in appetite, feeling physically slowed down or agitated, or even thoughts of not wanting to be here—compared to how you've been describing your day-to-day low feeling?

No, I don't think so. It's really just been... steady. I haven't had a time where it suddenly dropped and got a lot worse for a couple of weeks, or where I couldn't eat or wanted to hurt myself. It's just that same flat, drained feeling, day in and day out, for the whole three years. It doesn't really dip down into anything extreme, it just never really lets up either.

patient.answer: Yeah, I have. Most days, it just feels like there's this heavy, flat feeling following me around. It doesn't really go away. Even when I'm just at work, you know, pushing my cleaning cart down an empty hallway, it's right there with me. Or... even if I'm sitting at home with my family, just trying to act normal. It's just this constant, low feeling all the time.

inference.note: Added major depressive disorder (F32.9) and persistent depressive disorder (F34.1) as candidates given the newly reported persistent low mood, flat affect, and pervasive hopelessness that occur even outside shift-related contexts, which could account for the chronic fatigue and concentration problems independent of the sleep schedule.

doctor.intent: Determine duration of the depressive mood to distinguish an acute major depressive episode from chronic persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia)
doctor.question: You mentioned this low, flat feeling has been following you around—how long would you say you've been feeling this way, has it been more like a few weeks to months, or has it been going on almost continuously for two years or more?

target_item.name: Duration

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the patient has been feeling the low, flat feeling (depressed mood), specifically asking if it has been going on for a few weeks/months or continuously for two years or more. This directly relates to the 'duration' item.

patient.answer: It's definitely been more than two years. I'd say... it's been going on for about three years now. Yeah, about three years. It started right around the time the contractor changed us to rotating evening and overnight shifts at the larger properties. It's just been pretty continuous since then.

doctor.intent: Assess for additional major depressive episode symptoms (e.g., anhedonia severity, guilt, or thoughts of death) to distinguish a full major depressive episode from lower-grade chronic dysthymia
doctor.question: Besides the low, flat mood, have you noticed a loss of interest or pleasure in activities you used to enjoy, or any feelings of worthlessness or guilt?

target_item.name: Low_Self_Esteem
target_item.manifestation: I keep telling myself other guys would have adjusted by now and moved up, but I’m still just trying not to miss small things at work, so it makes me feel like maybe I’m not cut out for more than this.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question asks about loss of interest or pleasure, as well as feelings of worthlessness or guilt. The symptom profile includes 'Low_Self_Esteem' (feeling incompetent/worthless), which matches the 'worthlessness' part of the doctor's question.

patient.answer: Well, I don't know if I'd call it guilt, but... I definitely feel like I'm not measuring up. I keep telling myself that other guys would have adjusted to this schedule by now and probably moved up to something better. But I'm still just trying not to miss the small things at work, you know, just trying to keep my head above water. It really makes me feel like maybe I'm just not cut out for anything more than this.

inference.note: Continuous 3-year low mood with feelings of inadequacy support chronic depressive process (F34.1) possibly with superimposed major depressive episode (F32.9); persistent non-restorative sleep unrelieved by schedule freedom argues against primary shift-work/circadian disorder and keeps insomnia (F51.01) as either comorbid or symptom of the mood disorder.

doctor.intent: Assess for anhedonia specifically, to determine if loss of interest/pleasure in previously enjoyed activities is present, which is a core criterion helping distinguish major depressive episode from persistent depressive disorder or a primarily sleep-related mood disturbance
doctor.question: Have you lost interest or pleasure in activities you used to enjoy, like hobbies or spending time with family, over these past few months?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I still get the cleaning done, but I’m slower and second-guess my logs so much that I’ve stopped pushing for the supervisor track and I’ve been skipping neighborhood clean-ups and family get-togethers I used to make time for.

The 'Functional Impairment' item in the profile mentions skipping neighborhood clean-ups and family get-togethers they used to make time for, which directly addresses the doctor's question about losing interest in activities and spending time with family.

patient.answer: Yeah, I definitely have. I used to always make time for family get-togethers, or even these neighborhood clean-ups, but... I've just been skipping them lately. I don't really have the drive for it anymore. And it's kind of bleeding into everything else, too. Like at work, I still get the cleaning done, but I'm a lot slower now. I end up second-guessing my logs so much that I've actually just stopped pushing for the supervisor track altogether. I just don't have it in me right now.

inference.note: The patient's sleep disturbance persists regardless of shift schedule, time off, or sleep timing, arguing against a primary circadian/shift-work or insomnia disorder (F51.01) and suggesting the sleep complaints are secondary to a mood disorder. The 3-year history of continuous low, flat mood with recent superimposed anhedonia, loss of interest, feelings of inadequacy, and functional decline supports persistent depressive disorder (F34.1) with a current major depressive episode (F32.9), i.e., 'double depression.'

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has ever experienced a distinct 2-week (or longer) period where the depressive symptoms were markedly more severe—including changes in appetite/weight, psychomotor agitation or slowing, or thoughts of death/suicide—superimposed on the chronic low mood, which would indicate a major depressive episode rather than a purely persistent low-grade dysthymic pattern.
doctor.question: Over these past three years, has there ever been a stretch of two weeks or more where your mood, energy, or sleep got noticeably worse than your usual baseline—maybe with big changes in appetite, feeling physically slowed down or agitated, or even thoughts of not wanting to be here—compared to how you've been describing your day-to-day low feeling?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the presence of Major Depressive Episodes (a distinct period of 2 weeks or more with significantly worse symptoms like changes in appetite, psychomotor agitation/retardation, suicidal ideation) superimposed on the chronic low mood (double depression). The symptom profile does not contain a specific item for Major Depressive Episodes or the specific symptoms mentioned (appetite changes, psychomotor changes, suicidal thoughts).

patient.answer: No, I don't think so. It's really just been... steady. I haven't had a time where it suddenly dropped and got a lot worse for a couple of weeks, or where I couldn't eat or wanted to hurt myself. It's just that same flat, drained feeling, day in and day out, for the whole three years. It doesn't really dip down into anything extreme, it just never really lets up either.

inference.note: Patient denies any distinct 2-week period of acute worsening in mood/energy/sleep beyond the baseline; the low, flat mood has been continuous and non-episodic for 3 years, which is inconsistent with a major depressive episode (F32.9) and instead supports persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia).

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a chronic, continuous depressive mood lasting approximately 3 years, without discrete two-week episodes of worsening mood, appetite, or suicidality that would indicate superimposed major depressive episodes. Associated symptoms include low self-esteem/feelings of inadequacy, anhedonia (withdrawal from family gatherings and community activities), decreased concentration/energy, and chronic sleep disturbance. Extensive questioning ruled out shift-work/circadian rhythm sleep disorder (symptoms persist even during time off and with flexible sleep scheduling), sleep apnea, restless legs syndrome, hypothyroidism, and stimulant use as primary causes of the fatigue/concentration issues, suggesting these are secondary to the chronic mood disturbance. The persistent, low-grade, non-episodic nature of the depressive symptoms over 2+ years without meeting full criteria for a major depressive episode supports a diagnosis of Persistent Depressive Disorder (Dysthymia).
